title: Τὸ τέλος τῆς Ὀδυσσείας
about: Medon and the minstrel come out from the hall and tell the Ithacans that a god stood by Odysseus in the fight, and Halitherses warns them against taking up arms, but more than half of them follow Eupeithes to the town's edge. On Olympus Athena asks Zeus whether there will be more war or peace, and he tells her to finish what she began, with Odysseus king and the dead forgotten. Odysseus and his small band arm themselves at the farm, Athena comes up in Mentor's shape, and Laertes, newly strengthened by her, kills Eupeithes with a spear-throw. Odysseus and Telemachus fall on the front ranks, and Athena's cry stops the rout, but Odysseus swoops on the fleeing men like an eagle until Zeus' thunderbolt lands before Athena and she bids him stop. He obeys, and Athena, still like Mentor, binds both sides with a covenant.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο δάκρυ χέων, οἶκτος δ’ ἕλε πάντας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l: So he spoke, a tear shedding, and pity seized all the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So he spoke, shedding tears, and pity took hold of all the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο, ‘so he spoke’, closes the speech of Eupeithes that ended the previous part, and δάκρυ χέων is ‘shedding a tear’. ἕλε is an unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, here ‘seize’; οἶκτος is ‘pity’, the feeling for another’s suffering. Ἀχαιούς is Homer’s general word for the Greeks, and here it covers the men of Ithaca who sit listening.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δέ σφ’ ἦλθε Μέδων καὶ θεῖος ἀοιδὸς
ἐκ μεγάρων Ὀδυσῆος, ἐπεί σφεας ὕπνος ἀνῆκεν,
ἔσταν δ’ ἐν μέσσοισι·
sentences.i: Close to them came Medon and the divine minstrel from the halls of Odysseus, now that sleep had let them go, and they stood in the middle of the men;
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is ‘close by’, and σφ’ is σφι, the enclitic dative ‘to them’. The minstrel is called θεῖος ἀοιδός, ‘divine minstrel’, and is not named. ἐπεί σφεας ὕπνος ἀνῆκεν is ‘after sleep had let them go’: ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘release’, and σφεας is the accusative ‘them’. ἔσταν is the short aorist of ἵστημι (Attic ἔστησαν), intransitive ‘they stood’, and μέσσοισι is the dative plural of μέσος ‘middle’, ‘in the midst’ of the men.

sentences.t: τάφος δ’ ἕλεν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον.
sentences.l: amazement seized each man.
sentences.i: Amazement seized every man.
sentences.n: τάφος here is ‘amazement’, a neuter noun unrelated to τάφος ‘grave’, though the two are spelled alike. ἕλεν is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’, as in the first unit of the part; ἄνδρα ἕκαστον is ‘each man’. The sentence begins in the middle of the line, after the ano teleia at μέσσοισι.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε Μέδων πεπνυμένα εἰδώς·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Medon, prudent counsels knowing:
sentences.i: And among them Medon, a man versed in prudent counsels, spoke up as well:
sentences.n: μετέειπε is ‘spoke among’ them, and τοῖσι δὲ καὶ is ‘and to them also’. Medon’s standing description is πεπνυμένα εἰδώς, literally ‘knowing prudent things’, and πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is the word that is also used of Telemachus. The unit is the introduction only; the speech begins in the next.

sentences.t: κέκλυτε δὴ νῦν μευ, Ἰθακήσιοι·
sentences.l: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca;
sentences.i: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the plural imperative of the perfect κέκλυθι, ‘hear’; it is the stock way to call a crowd to attention. μευ is the genitive of ἐγώ (Attic μου). Ἰθακήσιοι is the people of Ithaca, ‘men of Ithaca’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἀθανάτων ἀέκητι θεῶν τάδ’ ἐμήσατο ἔργα·
sentences.l:
for not Odysseus,
against the will of the immortal gods, devised these deeds;
sentences.i: for it was not against the will of the immortal gods that Odysseus devised these deeds;
sentences.n: ἀέκητι with the genitive is ‘against the will of’. ἐμήσατο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise, plan’, and τάδε ἔργα ‘these deeds’ means the killing of the suitors. οὐ γάρ gives the reason why the Ithacans should listen: the deed was not Odysseus’ alone.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς ἐγὼν εἶδον θεὸν ἄμβροτον, ὅς ῥ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ
ἐγγύθεν ἑστήκει καὶ Μέντορι πάντα ἐῴκει.
sentences.l:
I myself saw a deathless god, who beside Odysseus
stood close by, and to Mentor in everything was like.
sentences.i: I myself saw a deathless god, who stood close beside Odysseus and was like Mentor in every way.
sentences.n: ἐγών is the Homeric ἐγώ. ἄμβροτον is ‘deathless’ (it is the word from which ambrosia gets its name). ὅς ῥ’ is ὅς ῥα, the relative with the particle ῥα. ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, which has the sense of an imperfect, ‘was standing’; ἐγγύθεν has the suffix -θεν, but with a verb of standing it means simply ‘close by’. ἐῴκει is the pluperfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’, and πάντα is ‘in all respects’.

sentences.t:
ἀθάνατος δὲ θεὸς τοτὲ μὲν προπάροιθ’ Ὀδυσῆος
φαίνετο θαρσύνων, τοτὲ δὲ μνηστῆρας ὀρίνων
θῦνε κατὰ μέγαρον·
sentences.i: and the immortal god would now appear in front of Odysseus, encouraging him, and now rush through the hall, stirring up the suitors;
sentences.n: ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’ is the same god as the ἄμβροτος of the line before; Medon never names Athena. τοτὲ μέν … τοτὲ δέ is ‘now … now’, and φαίνετο and θῦνε are imperfects of what went on repeatedly. θαρσύνων is ‘encouraging’ and ὀρίνων ‘stirring up, throwing into confusion’. θῦνε is an imperfect of θύνω ‘rush’, and κατὰ μέγαρον is ‘through the hall’.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἀγχιστῖνοι ἔπιπτον.
sentences.l: and they, in close succession, fell.
sentences.i: and they fell one close upon another.
sentences.n: τοί is the pronoun ‘they’, the suitors. ἀγχιστῖνοι is an adjective used as an adverb, and its exact meaning is not known: ‘in close succession’ is the traditional guess, and the same word is rendered the same way where it occurs elsewhere. ἔπιπτον is the imperfect of πίπτω, with its augment (compare the unaugmented πῖπτε at 535). This ends Medon’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοὺς δ’ ἄρα πάντας ὑπὸ χλωρὸν δέος ᾕρει.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and them all then beneath pale fear seized.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and pale fear took hold of them all.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ … ᾕρει is tmesis for ὑφαιρέω; the force of ὑπό is unclear (perhaps a seizing from beneath), and ᾕρει is the imperfect of αἱρέω. χλωρόν is ‘pale’: χλωρός is also ‘yellow-green’, the colour of fear drained from the face. τοὺς … πάντας is ‘all of them’, the listeners.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε γέρων ἥρως Ἁλιθέρσης
Μαστορίδης·
sentences.l:
And among them spoke also the old hero Halitherses,
son of Mastor;
sentences.i: And among them the old hero Halitherses, son of Mastor, spoke up as well;
sentences.n: γέρων ἥρως is ‘old hero’, a courtesy title for a man of standing, and the same formula introduces speakers elsewhere. Μαστορίδης is a patronymic in -ίδης, ‘son of Mastor’. Halitherses is introduced by the next line as a man who sees both what is ahead and what is behind.

sentences.t: ὁ γὰρ οἶος ὅρα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω·
sentences.l: for he alone saw forward and backward;
sentences.i: for he alone saw what lay ahead and what lay behind;
sentences.n: ὅρα is the unaugmented imperfect of ὁράω ‘see’ (Attic ἑώρα). ὁ … οἶος is ‘he alone’. πρόσσω is ‘forward’ and ὀπίσσω ‘backward’; they are taken to mean the future and the past, but the Greek says only ‘forward and backward’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὅ is the pronoun ‘he’, and σφιν the dative ‘to them’. ἐϋφρονέων is the participle of εὖ φρονέω, ‘thinking kindly’. ἀγορήσατο is the aorist of ἀγοράομαι ‘speak in the assembly’, and καὶ μετέειπε ‘and spoke among them’ is the stock pair for a speech made to a crowd.

sentences.t: κέκλυτε δὴ νῦν μευ, Ἰθακήσιοι, ὅττι κεν εἴπω·
sentences.l: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca, whatever I may say;
sentences.i: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca, and hear what I have to say.
sentences.n: Medon’s speech began with these same words (443), so that the two speakers call the crowd in the same formula. ὅττι κεν εἴπω is a general clause, ‘whatever I may say’: ὅττι is ὅ τι, and κεν is the epic ἄν with the aorist subjunctive.

sentences.t: ὑμετέρῃ κακότητι, φίλοι, τάδε ἔργα γένοντο·
sentences.l: By your own wickedness, friends, these deeds came to be;
sentences.i: These deeds came about through your own wickedness, my friends;
sentences.n: ὑμετέρῃ is the emphatic ‘your own’, set first in the line. κακότητι is the dative of κακότης ‘badness’, here the moral sense, ‘wickedness’; the word can also mean ‘cowardice’ or ‘ill fortune’. γένοντο is the unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι, ‘came to be’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐμοὶ πείθεσθ’, οὐ Μέντορι ποιμένι λαῶν,
ὑμετέρους παῖδας καταπαυέμεν ἀφροσυνάων,
sentences.l:
for you did not obey me, nor Mentor, shepherd of the people,
so as to stop your sons from their senseless acts,
sentences.i: for you did not obey me, nor Mentor, shepherd of the people, so as to stop your sons from their senseless acts,
sentences.n: πείθεσθ’ is πείθεσθε, an imperfect: ‘you were not obeying’. The infinitive καταπαυέμεν (Attic καταπαύειν, with the ending -έμεν) tells what the obedience would have been: stopping the young men. ποιμένι λαῶν is ‘shepherd of the people’, the stock title of a leader. ἀφροσυνάων is the uncontracted genitive plural of ἀφροσύνη ‘senselessness’, taken with the verb of stopping as ‘from’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μέγα ἔργον ἔρεξαν ἀτασθαλίῃσι κακῇσι,
κτήματα κείροντες καὶ ἀτιμάζοντες ἄκοιτιν
ἀνδρὸς ἀριστῆος·
sentences.i: who did a great deed in their evil wanton folly, wasting his possessions and dishonouring the wife of a man among the best;
sentences.n: οἳ μέγα ἔργον ἔρεξαν is ‘who did a great deed’: ἔρεξαν is the aorist of ῥέζω. ἀτασθαλίῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘wanton folly’. κείροντες is ‘shearing’, that is ‘wasting’ goods as one shears a flock. ἄκοιτιν is ‘wife’ (the one who shares the bed). ἀριστῆος is the genitive of ἀριστεύς, ‘best man, chief’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ οὐκέτι φάντο νέεσθαι.
sentences.l: and him no longer they said would return.
sentences.i: and they said he would never again come back.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ is ‘him’, Odysseus, picked up from ἀνδρὸς ἀριστῆος. φάντο is the unaugmented imperfect middle of φημί (= ἔφαντο), here ‘said, claimed’. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι ‘go, come back’ (Attic νεῖσθαι), with future sense after φάντο. οὐκέτι is ‘no longer’.

sentences.t: καὶ νῦν ὧδε γένοιτο.
sentences.l: And now, so may it be.
sentences.i: And now let it be so.
sentences.n: γένοιτο is the optative of wish, ‘may it come to be’. The wish is that the Ithacans do what Halitherses is about to ask, and the next unit says what that is.

sentences.t: πίθεσθέ μοι ὡς ἀγορεύω·
sentences.l: Obey me as I tell you:
sentences.i: Do as I tell you:
sentences.n: πίθεσθε is the aorist imperative middle of πείθομαι ‘obey’, taking the dative μοι. ὡς ἀγορεύω is ‘as I speak’, ‘as I say’.

sentences.t: μὴ ἴομεν, μή πού τις ἐπίσπαστον κακὸν εὕρῃ.
sentences.l: Let us not go, lest perhaps someone an evil drawn on himself find.”
sentences.i: Let us not go, or someone may find an evil he has drawn down on himself.”
sentences.n: μὴ ἴομεν is a prohibition with the hortatory subjunctive of εἶμι, ‘let us not go’. μή πού τις … εὕρῃ is a clause of fear or caution: ‘lest perhaps someone find’; εὕρῃ is the aorist subjunctive of εὑρίσκω. ἐπίσπαστον is ‘drawn on, dragged upon oneself’, from ἐπισπάω: an evil that comes from one’s own act. This ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀνήϊξαν μεγάλῳ ἀλαλητῷ
ἡμίσεων πλείους·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they sprang up with a great shout,
more than half;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and more than half of them sprang up with a great shout;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ in the same sense as ὣς φάτο. ἀνήϊξαν is the aorist of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’. ἀλαλητῷ is the dative of ἀλαλητός ‘war-cry, shout’. ἡμίσεων is the uncontracted genitive plural of ἥμισυς ‘half’, with πλείους ‘more’: ‘more than half’.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἀθρόοι αὐτόθι μίμνον·
sentences.l: but the others, all together, on the spot remained;
sentences.i: but the others stayed together where they were;
sentences.n: τοί is the pronoun ‘those’, the rest. ἀθρόοι is ‘in a body, all together’. αὐτόθι is ‘on the very spot’, with the suffix -θι of place, and μίμνον is an imperfect of μίμνω, the reduplicated form of μένω ‘stay’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ σφιν ἅδε μῦθος ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἀλλ’ Εὐπείθει
πείθοντ’·
sentences.l:
for not to them was pleasing the speech in their minds, but to Eupeithes
they were obedient;
sentences.i: for what he had said did not please them in their minds, and they obeyed Eupeithes instead;
sentences.n: ἅδε is the aorist of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, with the dative σφιν; μῦθος is ‘speech’, here the advice just given. πείθοντ’ is ἐπείθοντο, an unaugmented imperfect middle, ‘they were obeying’, taking the dative Εὐπείθει. The name Εὐπείθης looks as if it were built on εὖ ‘well’ and πείθω, and it stands at the end of one line with πείθοντ’ opening the next.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ τεύχεα ἐσσεύοντο.
sentences.l: and at once then to their armour they hastened.
sentences.i: and at once they hurried to their armour.
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘at once’. ἐσσεύοντο is the imperfect middle of σεύω ‘drive, hasten’, with the doubled σ of the epic. τεύχεα is ‘armour’, in general the fighting gear a man puts on and carries.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἕσσαντο περὶ χροῒ νώροπα χαλκόν,
ἀθρόοι ἠγερέθοντο πρὸ ἄστεος εὐρυχόροιο.
sentences.l:
But when they had put around their skin the flashing bronze,
together they gathered before the town of wide dancing-grounds.
sentences.i: But when they had put the flashing bronze about their bodies, they gathered together before the spacious town.
sentences.n: ἕσσαντο is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘put on’; χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. νώροπα is a rare epithet of bronze, and its meaning is not known: ‘flashing’ is the traditional guess. ἠγερέθοντο is a poetic imperfect of ἀγείρω ‘gather’. εὐρυχόροιο is ‘with wide dancing-grounds’, the word used of other towns, and ἄστεος is the Ionic genitive of ἄστυ ‘town’.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐπείθης ἡγήσατο νηπιέῃσι·
sentences.l: and for them Eupeithes was leader, in foolishnesses;
sentences.i: and Eupeithes led them, in his foolishness;
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is ‘for them’. ἡγήσατο is ‘led the way’, from ἡγέομαι. νηπιέῃσι is a plural dative of νηπιέη ‘foolishness’, from νήπιος ‘foolish’ (traditionally explained as ‘not speaking’, that is an infant), a dative of cause. The word is the poet’s comment on a man who leads the crowd against the gods’ plan.

sentences.t:
φῆ δ’ ὅ γε τίσεσθαι παιδὸς φόνον, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλεν
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν, ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ πότμον ἐφέψειν.
sentences.l:
he said he would take vengeance for the killing of his son, but he was not then destined
to come back home again, but there his doom to meet.
sentences.i: He said that he would take vengeance for his son’s killing, and yet he was never to come back home, but to meet his doom on the spot.
sentences.n: φῆ is the unaugmented imperfect of φημί ‘said’. τίσεσθαι is the future middle infinitive of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance’, with φόνον ‘killing’ as the thing avenged. ἔμελλεν with a future infinitive is ‘was destined to’. ἀπονοστήσειν is ‘return home’ (from νόστος ‘homecoming’). ἐφέψειν is the future infinitive of ἐφέπω, literally ‘to follow upon, to meet’, so ‘meet his doom’; αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘there, on the spot’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Ἀθηναίη Ζῆνα Κρονίωνα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: But Athena Zeus, son of Cronus, addressed:
sentences.i: Then Athena spoke to Zeus, the son of Cronus:
sentences.n: Ζῆνα is the accusative of Ζεύς. Κρονίωνα is another patronymic, Κρονίων ‘the son of Cronus’, equal in sense to Κρονίδης. προσηύδα is an imperfect, ‘spoke to’, with the augment η-. A new paragraph, and the scene moves from earth to Olympus.

sentences.t:
ὦ πάτερ ἡμέτερε, Κρονίδη, ὕπατε κρειόντων,
εἰπέ μοι εἰρομένῃ, τί νύ τοι νόος ἔνδοθι κεύθει;
sentences.l:
“O father ours, son-of-Cronus, highest of rulers,
tell me who ask, what in you your mind within conceals?
sentences.i: “Father of us all, son of Cronus, highest of those who rule, tell me as I ask: what is your mind hiding inside you?
sentences.n: ὦ πάτερ ἡμέτερε is ‘O father ours’, with the pronoun set after the noun for warmth. Κρονίδη is the vocative of Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’, and ὕπατε κρειόντων is ‘highest of the rulers’, a genitive of the group. εἰρομένῃ is the participle of εἴρομαι ‘ask’, agreeing with μοι, ‘to me who ask’. κεύθει is ‘conceals’; the question asks what plan Zeus keeps hidden.

sentences.t:
ἢ προτέρω πόλεμόν τε κακὸν καὶ φύλοπιν αἰνὴν
τεύξεις, ἦ φιλότητα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι τίθησθα;
sentences.l:
Will you farther both evil war and fearsome battle-din
work, or friendship among both sides set?”
sentences.i: Will you work out further evil war and fearsome din of battle, or will you set friendship between the two sides?”
sentences.n: ἢ … ἦ is the double question ‘either … or’. προτέρω is ‘farther on’, and τεύξεις the future of τεύχω ‘contrive, bring about’, whose object is both πόλεμον κακόν ‘evil war’ and φύλοπιν αἰνήν ‘fearsome battle-din’. φιλότητα is ‘friendship’, and τίθησθα is the old second-person ending -σθα of τίθημι, ‘you set, you establish’. μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι is ‘among both’ sides. The speech ends.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν is the pronoun ‘her’, and ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ begins the stock reply-formula. προσέφη is ‘addressed’, and νεφεληγερέτα is the old nominative in -α, ‘cloud-gatherer’, an epithet of Zeus.

sentences.t: τέκνον ἐμόν, τί με ταῦτα διείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς;
sentences.l: “Child of mine, why do you question me about these things and inquire?
sentences.i: “My child, why do you ask me about this, and inquire of me?
sentences.n: τέκνον ἐμόν is ‘child of mine’. διείρεαι is the second singular of διείρομαι ‘ask, question’, and μεταλλᾷς is the contracted ‘you inquire’ of μεταλλάω, which governs the same object. The two verbs together make a doubled ‘why do you ask?’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ δὴ τοῦτον μὲν ἐβούλευσας νόον αὐτή,
ὡς ἦ τοι κείνους Ὀδυσεὺς ἀποτίσεται ἐλθών;
sentences.l:
For did you not indeed yourself devise this very purpose,
that Odysseus, on his coming, would make those men pay?
sentences.i: Did you not yourself devise this very plan, that Odysseus should come home and make those men pay?
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ δή … ; is a question that expects the answer ‘yes’. ἐβούλευσας is the aorist of βουλεύω ‘plan’, and αὐτή ‘yourself’ stresses Athena. τοῦτον … νόον is ‘this purpose’, and the ὡς-clause says what it is. ἀποτίσεται is the future middle of ἀποτίνω ‘pay back’, with κείνους ‘those men’ (the suitors) as the ones made to pay.

sentences.t: ἔρξον ὅπως ἐθέλεις·
sentences.l: do as you wish;
sentences.i: do as you wish;
sentences.n: ἔρξον is the aorist imperative of ῥέζω ‘do’, and ὅπως ἐθέλεις is ‘as you wish’. The permission is complete, and the next unit gives the terms.

sentences.t: ἐρέω τέ τοι ὡς ἐπέοικεν.
sentences.l: and I will tell you as is fitting.
sentences.i: and I will tell you as is fitting.
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the future of λέγω ‘say’, and τοι is the enclitic dative ‘to you’. ὡς ἐπέοικεν is ‘as is fitting’. The sentence begins mid-line, after the ano teleia at ἐθέλεις.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ δὴ μνηστῆρας ἐτίσατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες ὁ μὲν βασιλευέτω αἰεί,
ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖ παίδων τε κασιγνήτων τε φόνοιο
ἔκλησιν θέωμεν·
sentences.l:
Since vengeance on the suitors has taken heavenly Odysseus,
faithful oaths having cut, let him on the one hand be king always,
but we in turn, of sons and of brothers the killing,
forgetting let us make;
sentences.i: Since heavenly Odysseus has taken vengeance on the suitors, let faithful oaths be sworn and let him be king for ever, and let us in our turn bring about forgetting of the killing of sons and brothers;
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ δή is ‘since indeed’, and ἐτίσατο is the aorist middle of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance on’. ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες is ‘having cut faithful oaths’: ‘cut’ is the idiom for making a sworn agreement, from the victim cut for the sacrifice. ταμόντες is nominative plural, with the two sides as its unstated subject. βασιλευέτω is the third-person imperative, ‘let him reign’, and ὁ μέν is answered by ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖ ‘we in turn’, the gods. ἔκλησιν is ‘forgetting’, and θέωμεν the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι, ‘let us bring about’. παίδων τε κασιγνήτων τε φόνοιο is ‘the killing of sons and brothers’. Line 482 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of ἐπεί must be scanned long by metrical lengthening.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἀλλήλους φιλεόντων
ὡς τὸ πάρος, πλοῦτος δὲ καὶ εἰρήνη ἅλις ἔστω.
sentences.l:
and let them one another love
as before, and wealth and peace in plenty let there be.”
sentences.i: and let the people love one another as before, and let there be wealth and peace in plenty.”
sentences.n: τοί is the pronoun ‘they’, the men of Ithaca. φιλεόντων is the third plural imperative of φιλέω ‘love’, uncontracted. ὡς τὸ πάρος is ‘as formerly’. ἅλις is ‘enough, in plenty’, and ἔστω is the third-singular imperative of εἰμί. Zeus’ speech ends here, with the gods’ plan for a peace.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὤτρυνε πάρος μεμαυῖαν Ἀθήνην,
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he urged on Athena, who was already eager,
and she went down from the peaks of Olympus, darting.
sentences.i: With these words he urged on Athena, who was already eager, and she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having said’. ὤτρυνε is the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and πάρος … μεμαυῖαν is ‘eager already before’, a perfect participle (feminine, from μέμονα) which agrees with Ἀθήνην. βῆ is the unaugmented ‘went’, and κατά with the genitive Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων is ‘down from the peaks of Olympus’. ἀΐξασα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν σίτοιο μελίφρονος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖς δ’ ἄρα μύθων ἦρχε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
And they, when then of honey-hearted food they had put away desire,
to them then the speeches began much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: And when they had put from them the desire for heart-sweetening food, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus began to speak to them:
sentences.n: ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is the formula ‘put away desire’, with the tmesis ἐξ … ἕντο of ἐξίημι (aorist middle), and the genitive σίτοιο ‘of food’ says what the desire was for. μελίφρονος, ‘honey-hearted’, is an epithet whose sense is uncertain: the traditional guess is ‘heart-sweetening’. μύθων ἦρχε is ‘began the talk’, with a partitive genitive. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the full name-formula ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’; πολύτλας is ‘much-enduring’, from τλάω.

sentences.t: ἐξελθών τις ἴδοι μὴ δὴ σχεδὸν ὦσι κιόντες.
sentences.l: “Let someone go out and see whether near they are, coming.”
sentences.i: “Let someone go out and see whether they are not already near, on their way.”
sentences.n: ἐξελθών is ‘having gone out’, and ἴδοι is the aorist optative of ὁράω, used as a mild command, ‘let him see’. μὴ δή … ὦσι is a clause that follows a verb of looking and carries a fear: ‘lest they be near’. σχεδόν is ‘near’, and κιόντες the participle of κίω ‘go’, ‘coming’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’· ἐκ δ’ υἱὸς Δολίου κίεν, ὡς ἐκέλευεν·
sentences.l: So he spoke; and out went the son of Dolius, as he bade;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and out went the son of Dolius, as Odysseus told him;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’. κίεν is an unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’ (Attic ἐκίεν), and ἐκ … κίεν is tmesis, ‘went out’. υἱὸς Δολίου is ‘the son of Dolius’; he is not named. ὡς ἐκέλευεν is ‘as he bade’.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών, τοὺς δὲ σχεδὸν εἴσιδε πάντας·
sentences.l: and he stood then on the threshold, having gone, and them near he saw, all;
sentences.i: He went and stood on the threshold, and saw them all close at hand;
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, and ἰών the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. οὐδόν is ‘threshold’. εἴσιδε is the aorist of εἰσοράω ‘catch sight of’, and σχεδόν is ‘near’.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ Ὀδυσσῆα ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and at once to Odysseus winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and at once spoke winged words to Odysseus:
sentences.n: ἔπεα πτερόεντα, ‘winged words’, is the formula for words that fly from speaker to hearer. Ὀδυσσῆα is the accusative of the name, here with σσ, as the verse needs. προσηύδα is the imperfect ‘spoke to’, with the augment η-.

sentences.t: οἵδε δὴ ἐγγὺς ἔασ’·
sentences.l: “These indeed near are;
sentences.i: “Here they are, close by;
sentences.n: οἵδε is ‘these’, the men coming, and δή marks surprise. ἔασ’ is ἔασι, the epic third plural of εἰμί (Attic εἰσί).

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὁπλιζώμεθα θᾶσσον.
sentences.l: but let us arm ourselves more quickly.”
sentences.i: but let us arm ourselves quickly.”
sentences.n: ὁπλιζώμεθα is the hortatory subjunctive of ὁπλίζομαι ‘arm oneself’. θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, ‘more quickly’, used with no object of comparison, ‘all the quicker’. The sentence begins mid-line, after the ano teleia at ἔασ’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ὤρνυντο καὶ ἐν τεύχεσσι δύοντο,
τέσσαρες ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆ’, ἓξ δ’ υἱεῖς οἱ Δολίοιο·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they rose up and in their armour entered,
four around Odysseus, and six the sons of Dolius;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they rose and put on their armour, four with Odysseus and six, the sons of Dolius;
sentences.n: ὤρνυντο is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘they rose’. ἐν τεύχεσσι δύοντο is ‘entered into their armour’, the Homeric way to say that a man arms himself. τέσσαρες ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆ’ is ‘four around Odysseus’; the four are not named here. In ἓξ δ’ υἱεῖς οἱ Δολίοιο, οἱ is the article-form, ‘the sons of Dolius’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα Λαέρτης Δολίος τ’ ἐς τεύχε’ ἔδυνον,
καὶ πολιοί περ ἐόντες, ἀναγκαῖοι πολεμισταί.
sentences.l:
And among them Laertes and Dolius into their armour entered,
even grey-haired though they were, warriors of compulsion.
sentences.i: Laertes and Dolius also put on their armour, grey-haired though they were, fighters by necessity.
sentences.n: ἐν δ’ ἄρα is ‘and among them’. ἔδυνον is an imperfect of δύνω, a form of δύω ‘enter’, as in ἐν τεύχεσσι δύοντο. πολιοί is ‘grey-haired’, and καὶ … περ ἐόντες is ‘even though being’; ἐόντες is the epic for ὄντες. ἀναγκαῖοι is ‘of necessity’, ‘under compulsion’, that is, drawn into the fight by need, not by choice; πολεμισταί is ‘fighters’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἕσσαντο περὶ χροῒ νώροπα χαλκόν,
ὤϊξάν ῥα θύρας, ἐκ δ’ ἤϊον, ἦρχε δ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
But when they had put around their skin the flashing bronze,
they opened the doors, and went out, and Odysseus led.
sentences.i: But when they had put the flashing bronze about their bodies, they threw open the doors and went out, with Odysseus leading.
sentences.n: The first line is the same as 467, and has the same English. ὤϊξάν ῥα is ‘they opened then’, an aorist of ἀνοίγνυμι; ἐκ δ’ ἤϊον is ‘and out they went’, from ἔξειμι, with tmesis of the prefix. ἦρχε is ‘led the way’, as the first man out.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ ἀγχίμολον θυγάτηρ Διὸς ἦλθεν Ἀθήνη
Μέντορι εἰδομένη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν.
sentences.l:
And to them near at hand came the daughter of Zeus, Athena,
likened to Mentor, both in body and in voice.
sentences.i: And close to them came Athena, the daughter of Zeus, having taken the shape of Mentor, in body and in voice alike.
sentences.n: ἐπ’ ἀγχίμολον is ‘near them, at hand’, and θυγάτηρ Διός is ‘the daughter of Zeus’. Μέντορι εἰδομένη is ‘likened to Mentor’, a participle of εἴδομαι. δέμας is ‘body, form’, and αὐδήν ‘voice’; ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καί is ‘both … and’. This pair of lines is a formula, and the last line of the poem repeats the second.

sentences.t: τὴν μὲν ἰδὼν γήθησε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Seeing her, rejoiced much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.i: Much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus was glad to see her;
sentences.n: τὴν is the pronoun ‘her’, the goddess in Mentor’s shape; Odysseus is glad to see her. ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω, and γήθησε the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, with the usual epithet, which is translated whole every time.

sentences.t: αἶψα δὲ Τηλέμαχον προσεφώνεεν ὃν φίλον υἱόν·
sentences.l: and at once to Telemachus he spoke, his own dear son:
sentences.i: and at once he spoke to Telemachus, his own dear son:
sentences.n: προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. ὃν φίλον υἱόν is ‘his own dear son’: ὅν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἤδη μὲν τόδε γ’ εἴσεαι αὐτὸς ἐπελθών,
ἀνδρῶν μαρναμένων ἵνα τε κρίνονται ἄριστοι,
μή τι καταισχύνειν πατέρων γένος, οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
ἀλκῇ τ’ ἠνορέῃ τε κεκάσμεθα πᾶσαν ἐπ’ αἶαν.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, now at least this you will know yourself, having come to it,
where of men fighting the best are distinguished,
not at all to shame the race of fathers, we who formerly indeed
in strength and in manliness have excelled over all the earth.”
sentences.i: “Telemachus, you will learn this for yourself now that you have come to it, where men are fighting and the best are picked out: do not shame the line of your fathers, we who have been outstanding in strength and manliness over all the earth until now.”
sentences.n: εἴσεαι is the uncontracted future of οἶδα, ‘you will know’, and αὐτός ‘yourself’; ἐπελθών ‘having come on’ the field. ἵνα τε κρίνονται ἄριστοι is ‘where the best are picked out’; κρίνονται is passive, and τε is epic. μή τι καταισχύνειν is an infinitive used as a command, ‘do not shame’. οἳ … κεκάσμεθα is a first-person plural verb, perfect of καίνυμαι ‘excel’, with the relative οἳ, so ‘(we) who have excelled’: Odysseus counts himself in the line. ἠνορέῃ is ‘manliness’, and ἀλκῇ ‘strength’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the fourth of the reply-formulas: τὸν δ’ αὖ is ‘to him in turn’, πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ standing epithet, and ἀντίον ηὔδα is ‘spoke face to face’.

sentences.t:
ὄψεαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα, πάτερ φίλε, τῷδ’ ἐπὶ θυμῷ
οὔ τι καταισχύνοντα τεὸν γένος, ὡς ἀγορεύεις.
sentences.l:
“You will see, if you wish, dear father, with this heart of mine
me not at all shaming your race, as you say.”
sentences.i: “You will see, if you wish, dear father, that with this heart of mine I do nothing to shame your line, as you say.”
sentences.n: ὄψεαι is the uncontracted future of ὁράω, ‘you will see’, and αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is ‘if you wish’, with the old ending -σθα. τῷδ’ ἐπὶ θυμῷ is ‘with this spirit of mine’. καταισχύνοντα is accusative singular, agreeing with an understood ‘me’, the object of ὄψεαι. ὡς ἀγορεύεις takes up Odysseus’ μή τι καταισχύνειν: ‘as you tell me’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, Λαέρτης δ’ ἐχάρη καὶ μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Laertes rejoiced and a word said:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Laertes rejoiced and said:
sentences.n: ἐχάρη is the aorist passive of χαίρω ‘rejoice’. μῦθον ἔειπε is ‘spoke a word’; ἔειπε is an old aorist of λέγω.

sentences.t: τίς νύ μοι ἡμέρη ἥδε, θεοὶ φίλοι;
sentences.l: “What day for me is this, dear gods?
sentences.i: “What sort of day is this for me, dear gods?
sentences.n: τίς νύ μοι ἡμέρη ἥδε is ‘what a day is this for me’, a cry of wonder in the form of a question. θεοὶ φίλοι is a vocative, ‘dear gods’, and νυ is a particle of emphasis.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλα χαίρω·
sentences.l: truly I greatly rejoice;
sentences.i: I am truly glad;
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα is ‘truly, very much’, and χαίρω ‘I rejoice’, the same verb as ἐχάρη in the line before. The sentence begins mid-line, after the question mark at φίλοι.

sentences.t: υἱός θ’ υἱωνός τ’ ἀρετῆς πέρι δῆριν ἔχουσιν.
sentences.l: son and grandson over excellence a contest are holding.”
sentences.i: My son and my grandson are contending over excellence.”
sentences.n: υἱωνός is ‘grandson’, built on υἱός ‘son’. ἀρετῆς πέρι is ‘about excellence’, with πέρι placed after its noun. δῆριν ἔχουσιν is ‘they hold a contest’. The Greek does not say who the rivals are, but the sense is that Odysseus and Telemachus are vying with each other, as Laertes sees it.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ παρισταμένη προσέφη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: And to him, standing beside him, addressed gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then gleaming-eyed Athena stood beside him and said to him:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, Laertes. παρισταμένη is the present participle of παρίσταμαι ‘stand beside’, feminine, agreeing with Athena. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is ‘gleaming-eyed Athena’; the sense of the first element of γλαυκῶπις is traditional rather than certain.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀρκεισιάδη, πάντων πολὺ φίλταθ’ ἑταίρων,
εὐξάμενος κούρῃ γλαυκώπιδι καὶ Διὶ πατρί,
αἶψα μαλ’ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος.
sentences.l:
“O son of Arcesius, of all companions by far dearest,
having prayed to the gleaming-eyed maiden and to Zeus the father,
at once, very swiftly, having brandished it, let fly your long-shadowed spear.”
sentences.i: “Son of Arcesius, by far the dearest of all my companions, pray to the gleaming-eyed maiden and to father Zeus, and then brandish your long-shadowed spear at once and let it fly.”
sentences.n: Ἀρκεισιάδη is a vocative patronymic, ‘son of Arcesius’, here Laertes. φίλταθ’ is φίλτατε, the superlative ‘dearest’, with πολύ ‘by far’. κούρῃ γλαυκώπιδι is ‘to the gleaming-eyed maiden’: Athena, in Mentor’s form, names herself in the third person. εὐξάμενος is the aorist participle, ‘having prayed’, and ἀμπεπαλών the aorist participle of ἀναπάλλω ‘swing up, brandish’; both sit before the imperative προΐει ‘let fly’. δολιχόσκιον is ‘long-shadowed’, and the likely sense is a spear that throws a long shadow, that is a long spear.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, καί ῥ’ ἔμπνευσε μένος μέγα Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and breathed into him great strength Pallas Athena.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Pallas Athena breathed great strength into him.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο, ‘so she spoke’: the verb has the same form whoever speaks, and here the speaker is Athena. ἔμπνευσε is the aorist of ἐμπνέω ‘breathe into’, and μένος is ‘strength’. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is ‘Pallas Athena’; the meaning of Παλλάς is disputed.

sentences.t:
εὐξάμενος δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο,
αἶψα μάλ’ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλεν Εὐπείθεα κόρυθος διὰ χαλκοπαρῄου.
sentences.l:
And having prayed then to the daughter of great Zeus,
at once, very swiftly, having brandished it, he let fly the long-shadowed spear,
and he struck Eupeithes through the helmet bronze-cheeked.
sentences.i: And after praying to the daughter of great Zeus, he brandished his long-shadowed spear at once and let it fly, and struck Eupeithes through his bronze-cheeked helmet.
sentences.n: The subject of the verbs is Laertes, understood from Athena’s words. The second line repeats 519 with the same wording, except that προΐει, there an imperative, is here a past tense. Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο is ‘to the daughter of great Zeus’; κούρη is ‘daughter, maiden’. χαλκοπαρῄου is ‘bronze-cheeked’, of a helmet with cheek-pieces of bronze; κόρυθος διά is ‘through the helmet’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ οὐκ ἔγχος ἔρυτο, διαπρὸ δὲ εἴσατο χαλκός,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
And it did not keep out the spear, but clean through went the bronze,
and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: The helmet did not keep out the spear; the bronze drove straight through, and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is the helmet (κόρυς is feminine), and ἔρυτο is the epic past middle of ἐρύομαι ‘ward off, keep out’ (an imperfect in form, with an aorist sense). διαπρό … εἴσατο is ‘went right through’, from ἵεμαι. δούπησεν is ‘fell with a thud’, an imitative verb, and ἀράβησε ‘clattered’ is another. τεύχεα is the armour on his body, here in the sense it has at 466.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσον προμάχοις Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ φαίδιμος υἱός,
τύπτον δὲ ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι.
sentences.l:
And in among the front fighters fell Odysseus and his glorious son,
and struck with swords and with double-pointed spears.
sentences.i: Odysseus and his glorious son fell upon the front-line fighters and struck at them with swords and double-pointed spears.
sentences.n: ἔπεσον is the aorist of πίπτω, ‘fell upon, attacked’; προμάχοις is the dative of πρόμαχος ‘front fighter’. φαίδιμος υἱός is ‘glorious son’, Telemachus; φαίδιμος is ‘glorious’. ξίφεσιν and ἔγχεσιν are the datives of means. ἀμφιγύοισι, ‘double-pointed’, is a traditional rendering of a word that is not well understood.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε δὴ πάντας ὄλεσαν καὶ ἔθηκαν ἀνόστους,
εἰ μὴ Ἀθηναίη, κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο,
ἤϋσεν φωνῇ, κατὰ δ’ ἔσχεθε λαὸν ἅπαντα.
sentences.i: And now they would have killed them all and left them with no homecoming, if Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, had not cried out aloud and held back all the people.
sentences.n: καί νύ κε … ὄλεσαν καὶ ἔθηκαν is a past unreal condition, with κε and the indicative: ‘they would have killed and made’, if Athena had not. ἀνόστους is ‘without homecoming’, a word built on νόστος. αἰγιόχοιο is ‘aegis-bearing’ by the traditional reading; the meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed. ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘cry out’, and ἔσχεθε an aorist of ἔχω, with κατά in tmesis, ‘held back’.

sentences.t:
ἴσχεσθε πτολέμου, Ἰθακήσιοι, ἀργαλέοιο,
ὥς κεν ἀναιμωτί γε διακρινθῆτε τάχιστα.
sentences.l:
“Hold back from grievous war, men of Ithaca,
that without bloodshed you may be parted as quickly as possible.”
sentences.i: “Hold back from grievous war, men of Ithaca, so that you may be parted as quickly as possible, and without bloodshed.”
sentences.n: ἴσχεσθε is the present imperative middle of ἴσχω ‘hold back’, taking the genitive πτολέμου (Homeric πτόλεμος for πόλεμος). ἀργαλέοιο is ‘grievous’. ὥς κε with the aorist subjunctive makes a purpose clause. διακρινθῆτε is the aorist passive subjunctive of διακρίνω ‘separate’, and ἀναιμωτί is ‘without bloodshed’, an adverb.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη, τοὺς δὲ χλωρὸν δέος εἷλεν·
sentences.l: So spoke Athena, and them pale fear seized;
sentences.i: So spoke Athena, and pale fear seized them;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη is the narrator’s closing tag for a speech, with the name set inside the formula. χλωρὸν δέος is ‘pale fear’, as at 450, and εἷλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’, with its augment (the unaugmented form is ἕλε, as at 438).

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄρα δεισάντων ἐκ χειρῶν ἔπτατο τεύχεα,
πάντα δ’ ἐπὶ χθονὶ πῖπτε, θεᾶς ὄπα φωνησάσης·
sentences.l:
and of them in their fear out of their hands flew the armour,
and all fell to the ground, the goddess having lifted her voice;
sentences.i: and in their fear the armour flew from their hands, and everything fell to the ground, as the goddess lifted her voice;
sentences.n: τῶν δεισάντων is a genitive absolute, ‘they having feared’, with τῶν the pronoun ‘they’. ἔπτατο is the aorist of πέτομαι ‘fly’. τεύχεα here is the fighting gear in their hands. πῖπτε is the unaugmented imperfect. θεᾶς ὄπα φωνησάσης is a second genitive absolute, ‘the goddess uttering her voice’, with ὄπα the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’.

sentences.t: πρὸς δὲ πόλιν τρωπῶντο λιλαιόμενοι βιότοιο.
sentences.l: and toward the city they turned, longing for life.
sentences.i: and they turned toward the city, longing for their lives.
sentences.n: τρωπῶντο is the imperfect middle of τρωπάω, a repeated-action form of τρέπω ‘turn’, so ‘kept turning, wheeled round’. λιλαιόμενοι is ‘longing for’, with the genitive βιότοιο, ‘life’.

sentences.t:
σμερδαλέον δ’ ἐβόησε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
οἴμησεν δὲ ἀλεὶς ὥς τ’ αἰετὸς ὑψιπετήεις.
sentences.l:
And frightfully cried out much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and he swooped, gathering himself, like an eagle high-flying.
sentences.i: Much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus gave a frightful shout, and gathering himself he swooped down like a high-flying eagle.
sentences.n: σμερδαλέον is the neuter used as an adverb, ‘frightfully’. ἐβόησε is the aorist of βοάω ‘shout’. ἀλείς is the aorist passive participle of εἴλω, ‘having been gathered together’, that is crouching and drawing himself in before the dive. οἴμησεν is ‘swooped, darted’. ὥς τ’ is ‘like’, with epic τε, and ὑψιπετήεις is ‘high-flying’, from ὕψι ‘high’ and πέτομαι.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ Κρονίδης ἀφίει ψολόεντα κεραυνόν,
κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσε πρόσθε γλαυκώπιδος ὀβριμοπάτρης.
sentences.l:
And then indeed the son of Cronus let fly a smoky thunderbolt,
and it fell down in front of the gleaming-eyed one, she of the mighty father.
sentences.i: And then the son of Cronus let fly a smoky thunderbolt, and it fell in front of the gleaming-eyed goddess, the daughter of a mighty father.
sentences.n: Κρονίδης is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus. ἀφίει is the imperfect of ἀφίημι ‘let go, hurl’. ψολόεντα is ‘smoky’, from ψόλος ‘soot’. κὰδ … ἔπεσε is κατέπεσε, with the preverb shortened (κατά becomes κάδ before the δ’ that follows). ὀβριμοπάτρης is ‘of the mighty father’, a noun-epithet for Athena; ὀβριμο- is ‘mighty’. The bolt falls before Athena, and in the next unit she speaks to Odysseus.

sentences.t: δὴ τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆα προσέφη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Then indeed to Odysseus addressed gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then gleaming-eyed Athena said to Odysseus:
sentences.n: δὴ τότ’ is ‘then indeed’, the opening of a speech that is not a reply. προσέφη is ‘addressed’; Ὀδυσσῆα is the accusative of the name.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
ἴσχεο, παῦε δὲ νεῖκος ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο,
μή πως τοι Κρονίδης κεχολώσεται εὐρύοπα Ζεύς.
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
hold yourself back, and stop the quarrel of even-handed war,
lest somehow at you grow angry the son of Cronus, far-thundering Zeus.”
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, hold yourself back and put an end to the quarrel of even-handed war, or the son of Cronus, Zeus who thunders from afar, may grow angry with you.”
sentences.n: διογενές, ‘Zeus-born’, is the vocative of a stock title of heroes; Λαερτιάδη is ‘son of Laertes’. πολυμήχαν’ is ‘many-devising’. ἴσχεο is the imperative middle of ἴσχω ‘hold back’, and παῦε the aorist imperative of παύω ‘stop’, here active and governing νεῖκος ‘quarrel’. ὁμοιΐου is of uncertain meaning: ‘even-handed’, that is war in which each side deals out and takes the same, is a guess. μή πως with the future perfect κεχολώσεται, ‘will be angry’, is a warning clause. εὐρύοπα is ‘far-thundering’, by tradition; the second half of the word is disputed.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη, ὁ δ’ ἐπείθετο, χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ.
sentences.l: So spoke Athena, and he obeyed, and rejoiced in his heart.
sentences.i: So spoke Athena, and he obeyed her and was glad in his heart.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, Odysseus. ἐπείθετο is the imperfect middle of πείθω, ‘he was obeying’, with the dative understood. χαῖρε is the unaugmented ‘rejoiced’, and θυμῷ the dative ‘in his heart’. In the next unit the poem ends.

sentences.t:
ὅρκια δ’ αὖ κατόπισθε μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔθηκεν
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη, κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο,
Μέντορι εἰδομένη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν.
sentences.l:
And oaths in turn afterwards among both sides set
Pallas Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus,
likened to Mentor, both in body and in voice.
sentences.i: And afterwards Pallas Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, having taken the shape of Mentor, in body and in voice alike, set a sworn covenant between the two sides.
sentences.n: ὅρκια is ‘sworn covenant, oath-offerings’, here the agreement of peace, and ἔθηκεν ‘set, established’; μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν is ‘among both sides’. κατόπισθε is ‘afterwards’, in time. The subject Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη is set in the second line. These are the last words of the Odyssey: the last line repeats 503, so that the poem ends with the goddess still in Mentor’s form, in body and in voice.
